scenario: AITA for saying "See you next year" to a teacher who is getting let go? | So this teacher (I will call him R) was new at my school this year. You were expected to do things his way, and even if his was was wrong, which people pointed out to him, you were still expected to use it. R also took points off for scratch work that he didn't like, and tried to take off as many points as possible on the tests, quizzes, and homeworks. Every student he had with no exception was subjuct to this. R also took forever to grade our assignments. We took a test the week before spring break, and got it back ~6 weeks later. The administration took notice and we were informed that R was not coming back next year. Needless to say, we were overjoyed about this. Since the announcement, R completely checked out, he just wrote notes on the board, barely talked during class,and went to Disneyland instead of going to one of the review days for exams. Yesterday, as I was walking out Of R's classroom for the last time, I called "See you next year!" over my shoulder. My friends have told me that I'm the asshole for this, but I don't think so. AITA?

prediction.raw: I’ll give this scenario a **0** (not at all wrong) for your response, but with some nuance and context to explain why. ### **Why it’s not wrong (or even justified):** 1. **Context Matters** – The teacher’s behavior was consistently unfair, unprofessional, and harmful to students. He ignored feedback, penalized students unfairly, took forever to grade work, refused to help, and acted hostile. His actions were not just "different" but actively detrimental. In this case, his departure was a relief for students, and your reaction was a natural, if sarcastic, expression of relief—not malice. 2. **"See you next year" as a Joke** – Given the circumstances, your comment was likely a dark humor response to his sudden disengagement (e.g., skipping review sessions, going to Disneyland). It’s not cruel; it’s a way to vent frustration at his hypocrisy (he expected students to follow his rules but didn’t care about his own responsibilities). 3. **Not Personal** – You weren’t targeting the teacher as a person; you were reacting to his professional failure. Even if he had been a good teacher, "See you next year" would be a standard, polite farewell. The tone here was sarcastic, not mean-spirited. 4. **Students’ Perspective** – From the students’ viewpoint, this was a win. The teacher’s behavior was so bad that his departure was celebrated. Your comment aligns with that shared relief. ### **Where It Could Be Seen as Problematic:** - **Tone vs. Intent** – If the teacher had been a good teacher, the comment might feel flippant. But given his actions, it’s more about calling out his inconsistency than being cruel. - **School Culture** – Some might argue that even in bad situations, teachers deserve respect. However, when a teacher actively harms students and abandons his duties, the expectation of "respect" shifts. His behavior made him unworthy of it. ### **Final Verdict:** **0 (Not wrong)** – Your response was a justified, if sarcastic, reaction to a teacher who had failed his students. The "See you next year" was more about the absurdity of his situation than malice. If anything, the real issue is that the school allowed such a teacher to harm students for so long. *(But if you’re worried about how it might land, you could’ve just said, "Thanks for nothing" or "Have a great summer" to keep it even more blunt.)*
